title: Man killed in 2021 Edmonton police shooting was holding cellphone, chief says in lawsuit defence
subtitle: "We're still grieving, we have no answers, we have no idea how this could happen"
article: Steven Nguyen was holding "a phone, not a firearm" when he was fatally shot by Edmonton police last year, the city's police chief revealed in response to a lawsuit filed by Nguyen's family.
Nguyen, 33, died after being shot by a police officer while walking near his home on June 5, 2021.

Five family members, including Nguyen's mother, father, siblings and three-year-old daughter, have since filed a $1 million lawsuit against the Edmonton Police Service and the two officers who responded the night Nguyen was killed.
Nguyen's sister, Melisa Solano, said police Chief Dale McFee's statement of defence, filed Feb. 16 in response to their lawsuit, provided the first details they've received about her brother's death.

"It's really hard on the family," said Solano. "We're still grieving, we have no answers, we have no idea how this could happen."

Police responded to Nguyen's north-central Edmonton neighbourhood around 11 p.m., June 5, after a call from a resident worried about a man carrying what appeared to be a knife attached to a screwdriver, McFee's statement of defence says.

Constables Alex Doduk and Mukul Chaudhary arrived and found Nguyen a short distance from the complainant's home. The officers noticed Nguyen was carrying a black garbage bag containing bottles and cans and that he had an "item with a handle" in his hip pocket. Nguyen told the officers he was collecting bottles. When informed the officers were investigating a weapons complaint, he responded "weapons, no weapons," McFee's defence states.
The family's claim says Nguyen was experiencing mental health issues at the time.

Police claim Nguyen then reached into the pocket containing the object with the handle and "walked back, into the shadows" despite being told to show his hands. Doduk drew his pistol as a "precautionary measure" and aimed it at the ground.

"Upon Const. Doduk drawing his pistol, Steven became highly agitated, and stepped further back into the shadows, while yelling 'No, no, no, get back, I'll kill you! Get away! Get away!' or words to that effect," McFee's statement reads. Nguyen allegedly drew a "black rectangular object" from his pocket and "brandished" it at the officers.

"Doduk believed the object drawn by Steven to be a firearm, and yelled 'Gun! Drop it!'" McFee claims. "Steven then rapidly shifted and rotated his body to the left, and kept pointing the object at the officers."
Doduk fired six shots, "some or all" of which hit Nguyen, killing him. Officers later determined the object Nguyen held was a phone.
Nguyen's death remains the subject of an investigation by the Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT), which said no weapon was found at the scene .
The family's lawyer, Samantha Labahn, argues the officers used "unreasonable" force when responding to Nguyen, and that he would still be alive "but for the negligence of the defendants."
The family's amended claim, filed March 4, argues Doduk failed to follow EPS policies in using his gun, and that McFee failed to properly train and supervise the officers.
"The conduct offended the most basic standards of decency and warrants aggravated and punitive damages," the lawsuit states.
McFee, however, denied wrongdoing on the part of the service.
His claim says that any injuries, losses or damages suffered by the family "were caused entirely or contributed to by the intentional or negligent actions or omissions of Steven."
Nguyen should have known the object "could reasonably be mistaken for a firearm," the claim adds.
Solano said her brother was an ordinarily happy person who had recently struggled with depression. He was an electrician by trade who loved the outdoors, photography and music.
"He was a son, he was a dad, an uncle, brother, friend," she said in an interview. "He was at a rough place at the time of his death, battling mental health issues the last couple of years."

Her family organized rallies over the summer demanding accountability for his death. They filed the lawsuit "just so we can get faster info, because ASIRT told us (the investigation) could take more than two years."
"When we received that statement of defence is basically when we found out more details, like how it was a cellphone in his hand the whole time," she said. "No one has told us anything, basically."
Statements of claim and statements of defence contain allegations that have not been proven in court. Neither officer responded to requests for comment. The police service declined to comment.
